Moshi’s architecture is built around three core modules.  
The first is **Helium**, a bespoke text language‑model backbone that provides the system with strong linguistic knowledge and enables the “Inner Monologue” capability for aligned text generation [S1].  
The second is **Mimi**, a neural audio codec that uses residual‑vector quantisation and distills semantic knowledge from a self‑supervised speech model, turning speech into hierarchical semantic and acoustic token streams [S1][S7].  
The third component is the **streaming, hierarchical token generation** framework, which jointly produces semantic and acoustic tokens for both the user and Moshi (with time‑aligned text tokens when Inner Monologue is used), allowing real‑time, full‑duplex spoken dialogue [S1][S6].

record.text:
Moshi is full‑duplex because it models two separate streams of semantic and acoustic tokens—one for the user and one for the system—so it can listen and speak simultaneously rather than waiting for turn boundaries【S3】.  
Its multi‑stream Transformer architecture processes these parallel audio token streams jointly, allowing the model to generate and consume speech in real time without a fixed speaker‑turn schedule【S2】.  
By hierarchically streaming both semantic and acoustic tokens for each side, Moshi can align and interleave the user’s incoming speech with its own outgoing speech, handling overlapping utterances directly【S3】.  
The “Inner Monologue” component predicts time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, which further enables continuous streaming generation while still extracting linguistic information from the user’s side【S8】.  
Thus, Moshi’s dual‑stream token representation and streaming hierarchical generation together give it the capability to manage both participants speaking at once in a real‑time dialogue【S7】.

record.text: Inner Monologue is the mechanism in Moshi that jointly models a stream of text tokens and a stream of audio tokens, allowing the model to “talk to itself’’ by continuously generating and conditioning on both modalities within a single language‑model‑like sequence [S5][S2]. By inserting a controllable delay between the two token streams, the model can be made to decide which modality leads the other: if audio tokens are delayed relative to text, the text stream dictates the generated speech (streaming TTS); if text tokens are delayed relative to audio, the audio stream is listened to first and then used to generate transcription (streaming ASR) [S1][S3]. For streaming TTS the training uses a 2‑second delay of audio tokens, giving the model look‑ahead on text and teacher‑forcing the text tokens at inference time, so that speech is produced with low latency [S1]. For streaming ASR the training delays the text tokens by the same 2‑second amount, allowing the model to ingest audio before emitting text and then teacher‑forcing the audio tokens at inference [S1]. Changing only this single delay hyper‑parameter switches the same Moshi model between TTS and ASR without any architectural, loss‑function, or data changes [S2][S7]. Thus Inner Monologue provides a unified, delay‑controlled framework for deriving both streaming speech synthesis and streaming speech recognition from one model.

record.text: Inner Monologue is a modeling approach in Moshi that jointly streams text and audio tokens, allowing the language model to process and generate both modalities in a single unified sequence [S5]. By inserting a configurable delay between the two token streams, the model can be made to prioritize one modality over the other [S3]. For streaming TTS, audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) so that the model receives future text tokens as look‑ahead before generating audio, and at inference the text tokens are teacher‑forced [S1]. For streaming ASR, text tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) so that the model can listen to upcoming audio before emitting text, and at inference the audio tokens are teacher‑forced [S1]. The same loss, architecture, and training data are used for both tasks, with only the delay hyper‑parameter switched to move between ASR and TTS [S2]. This delay‑controlled Inner Monologue thus enables zero‑shot derivation of streaming speech synthesis and recognition from a single model [S8].

record.text:
The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions that either keep almost all vectors (defeating compression) or discard too much information (losing important content) by explicitly encouraging a target compression ratio [S3].  
In this loss, F represents the average fraction of selected vectors (e.g., boundary decisions) across the sequence, computed as the mean of the binary selection indicators bₜ over all timesteps t [S3].  
G denotes the average fraction of predicted probabilities pₜ for those selections, i.e., the mean of the routing probabilities across the sequence [S3].  
N is the total number of possible slots (or experts) that could be selected, appearing in the denominator that scales the desired compression proportion [(N−1)F G + (1−F)(1‑G)] [S3].  
When F and G are equal, the loss attains its minimum value of 1 (at F = G = 1/N), which encourages the model to balance its utilization and achieve the intended compression ratio [S5].  
If F and G deviate, the loss can drop below 1, but in practice the architecture pushes F ≈ G, so the ratio loss effectively guides the model toward the desired compression behavior [S5].

record.text: The experiments include a simple baseline that pools every k tokens (H‑Net (pool)), which is expected to be weaker than any data‑dependent chunking strategy [S2]. Validation results show that H‑Net (pool) performs much worse than the learned dynamic‑chunking variants, confirming that fixed‑width pooling is not effective [S7]. The full one‑stage dynamic model (H‑Net (1‑stage)) outperforms the pooling baseline, demonstrating the benefit of learned chunk boundaries [S2]. Adding a second nested stage (H‑Net (2‑stage)) further improves performance over the one‑stage variant, indicating that deeper dynamic hierarchies yield consistent gains [S6].
